planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Monsieur Tillier is an 1891 French tea rose valued in Deep South gardens for its vigorous, drought-tolerant growth and reliable performance in poor soil where many modern roses fail.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, spacing plants 3-4 feet apart to allow for its large, vigorous size. Introduced in France in 1891, Monsieur Tillier is a robust tea rose bearing large, loosely double blooms in variable shades of pink, salmon, and copper-tan, often several tones within a single flush, with a fruity tea fragrance. It is among the most drought-tolerant and vigorous of the old tea roses, capable of growing into a large shrub 5-6 feet tall and wide, and performs remarkably well in poor, sandy, or infertile soil where many modern roses struggle, a trait that made it a favorite for unattended cemetery and homestead plantings across the Deep South. It shows strong resistance to blackspot and thrives with minimal spraying in the humid Gulf South climate. Prune lightly in late winter to control size and remove dead or crossing wood, since Monsieur Tillier tolerates hard pruning better than many teas if size needs to be reduced.
sources: The Antique Rose Emporium — Monsieur Tillier variety notes
American Rose Society — Tea Rose Class Descriptions
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Old Garden Rose Collections

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container trees in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Trazels are hybrids between American hazelnut and the Turkish tree hazel, bred to grow as a single-trunked tree rather than a suckering shrub while carrying strong resistance to Eastern filbert blight, the fungal disease that devastates orchard plantings of European hazelnut through much of North America.

directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, allowing 15-25 feet between trees for their eventual size. Trazels are named for their parentage — a cross between the native American hazelnut (Corylus americana) and the Turkish tree hazel (Corylus colurna) — combining the American parent's cold hardiness and blight resistance with the Turkish parent's strong single-trunk, tree-like growth habit, unlike the suckering thicket form typical of most hazelnuts. This tree form makes Trazels far easier to manage in an orchard row or as a landscape specimen than shrubby hazelnut types, and their resistance to Eastern filbert blight — a fungal canker disease that has devastated commercial plantings of European hazelnut (C. avellana) across much of the eastern and midwestern United States — makes them one of the more dependable hazelnut options outside the Pacific Northwest. Nuts are borne in husked clusters and ripen in late summer to early fall; because most Trazel seedlings show variable nut size and quality, growers select and propagate individual trees for improved nut characteristics. Plant two or more seedlings for best pollination, since hazelnuts are wind-pollinated and largely self-incompatible.
sources: Badgersett Research Corporation — Hybrid Hazelnut Breeding Notes
University of Nebraska-Lincoln — Hazelnut Breeding for the Midwest
Arbor Day Foundation — Hazelnut Tree Selection Guide

common_name: Black Diamond Crape Myrtle (Dark Purple-Black Foliage Reblooming Series)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Black Diamond is a series distinguished from other crape myrtles by near-black, deep purple-maroon foliage that holds its color through the growing season, providing strong contrast against its bright summer flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Black Diamond is a series of crape myrtles bred for foliage that emerges near-black and holds its deep purple-maroon color through summer heat rather than fading to green, a trait that sets it apart from the many crape myrtle series bred primarily for flower color or mildew resistance. Individual selections within the series bloom in shades from pure white through pink, red, and purple, and the dark foliage makes even pale flower colors read as especially vivid by contrast. Like other modern interspecific crape myrtles (Lagerstroemia indica x fauriei), Black Diamond selections generally show good resistance to powdery mildew, an important trait in the humid Gulf South where older all-indica cultivars mildew heavily. Plants rebloom over several weeks if spent flower clusters are removed, and the naturally attractive, often multi-trunked form with exfoliating bark provides winter interest after leaf drop. Avoid the practice of severe annual 'crape murder' pruning, which sacrifices the plant's natural vase shape and delays bloom; instead remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches in late winter.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection — Black Diamond Crape Myrtle series notes
Clemson Cooperative Extension — Crape Myrtle Cultivar Selection
North Carolina State Extension — Crape Myrtle Culture

common_name: Vintage Jade Distylium (Compact Spreading Evergreen Shade Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Vintage Jade is a compact, wide-spreading distylium selection that stays under 4 feet tall while spreading considerably wider, useful as a durable evergreen groundcover-like shrub in deep shade where few broadleaf evergreens perform well.

directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Vintage Jade is a low, wide-spreading distylium selection that matures to roughly 3-4 feet tall but spreads 5-8 feet across, making it one of the most useful large-scale evergreen groundcover shrubs for difficult shady sites where azaleas, boxwood, and other traditional shade shrubs often struggle. Like other distyliums, it produces small, glossy, leathery, dark green leaves and inconspicuous, petal-less red-stamened flowers in late winter that add subtle color before most shrubs break dormancy. Its defining feature is extraordinary adaptability — it tolerates full sun, deep shade, wet or dry soil, and both acid and moderately alkaline pH with no serious pest or disease problems and virtually no pruning required to look tidy, and deer generally leave it alone. Because it spreads wider than tall, space plants according to their eventual width rather than the young nursery size, and use it in mass plantings, foundation beds, or as a substitute where foundation shrubs have failed in a heavily shaded spot.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Distylium Cultivar Notes
University of Georgia Extension — Low-Maintenance Evergreen Shrubs
Clemson Cooperative Extension — Distylium in the Southern Landscape

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, well away from gardens and other juglone-sensitive plants; Lamb is a named black walnut cultivar selected for a strong combination of nut size, cracking quality, and consistent annual production.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, sited well away from tomatoes, apples, and other plants sensitive to the juglone this species releases into the surrounding soil. Lamb is a named black walnut selection valued by nut growers for combining good kernel percentage and cracking quality with strong, consistent annual bearing, an important trait in a species that can otherwise produce heavily only every second year. Like other grafted black walnut cultivars, it grows into a large, long-lived shade tree over time, so it is best suited to a large property, orchard row, or field edge rather than a small home garden. Nuts drop in a thick, dark, staining husk in early fall that should be removed promptly to prevent kernel discoloration, and grafted trees typically begin bearing within six to ten years, considerably sooner than seedling trees. Rake and dispose of fallen husks away from lawns and walkways, since they stain concrete and skin on contact.
sources: Northern Nut Growers Association — Black Walnut Cultivar Trials
University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry
